source.title: LLMs Can Annotate Attribution Graphs
source.authors: Ameen Patel; Max Zhang; Nathan Hu

record.tranche_reason: The study compares automated grouping of raw MLP neurons with transcoder features and reports that a much smaller fraction of neurons is grouped, which the authors interpret as evidence that many MLP neurons lack a clean concept. This refines the broad claim that neurons are generally interpretable units, but does not reproduce the Qwen3-32B audit.
record.gate_note: The directly relevant reported outcome is the fraction of features grouped in the Capitals graphs for MLP neurons versus transcoder features. The 97-of-100 intermediate-hop recovery and causal patching results concern transcoder supernodes, not the raw-neuron audit claim. The study does not report a distribution of neurons with one job, two jobs, or not-yet-understood poles.
record.test_reason: The study is about an LLM pipeline that groups attribution-graph nodes into supernodes in Gemma-2-2B. The only neuron result is an appendix check that the pipeline generalizes to raw MLP neurons. The fraction of nodes grouped measures whether a node is relevant to the prompt's story and fits a group; the prompts explicitly send weak, grammatical or off-topic nodes to Ungrouped and say Ungrouped is not a failure. It does not measure whether each neuron (pole) has one main job, so it cannot show V2's shares. The comparison is also confounded: MLP graphs keep 150 nodes against about 45 for transcoder graphs, a number chosen to equalize grouped counts, so the MLP set includes many lower-influence nodes. The authors' remark that many MLP neurons lack a clean concept is an interpretation of this proxy, not a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it overweights an appendix aside. The main conclusion is that a simple, cheap LLM pipeline produces supernodes that score as interpretable as human annotations on autointerp metrics. It recovers the intermediate hop in 97 of 100 Capitals prompts and can flag interesting graphs. The MLP-neuron comparison (21.6% vs 60.2% grouped) is presented as a generalization check, with the remark that many MLP neurons may lack a clean concept. Limitations are one model, limited tasks, a single annotator, and arithmetic labels too coarse despite good autointerp scores.
record.recipe_differences: Uses feature descriptions generated from activating examples and token-logit information, then LLM grouping and automated validation; for raw neurons it separately describes positive- and negative-firing behavior. It does not reproduce the Qwen3-32B pole audit or its reported job-count categories.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported grouping fraction differs by basis: raw MLP neurons versus single-layer transcoder features. For the MLP-neuron comparison, the authors retain the top 150 neurons per graph after attribution-magnitude pruning.

fits_no_version.finding: In Gemma-2-2B Capitals graphs, the LLM grouping pipeline places 21.6% of the top-150 raw MLP neurons into supernodes versus 60.2% of transcoder features. The authors read this as suggesting many MLP neurons lack a clean concept.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In attribution graphs, automated description-and-grouping pipelines assign a smaller fraction of raw MLP neurons (signed, described per sign) to prompt-relevant concept groups than transcoder features, at matched grouped counts.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
record.problems: Only Gemma-2-2B is studied, and the raw-neuron result is on Capitals graphs. Grouping into supernodes is only an indirect proxy for whether each neuron pole has one main job; the paper does not report the claim's job-count categories or independently score neuron explanations on unseen activations. The authors also state that the pipeline is tested with a single LLM annotator.
record.rows_left_out: The 97-of-100 intermediate-hop recovery and the constrained-patching results in Section 4 concern transcoder supernodes, not raw MLP neuron interpretability. Appendix F figures 14–15 show example missing supernodes but do not report an aggregate neuron result beyond the grouped-fraction comparison.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B pole audit or job-count shares.
No one-job/two-job/unknown shares for any model; only Gemma-2-2B and only a grouping-rate proxy.
No vision models or canonical polysemantic neuron examples.
No manipulation of architecture, regularization or tools affecting neuron interpretability.
Neuron graphs are built with ADAG, but there is no test that they explain behaviour without a replacement model. Causal patching is done only on transcoder supernodes.
No test of whether neuron explanations from activating examples predict firing elsewhere.
No simulation scoring of neuron explanations. Per-feature description and text-detection scores (79.9%/85.4%) are for transcoder features and are discrimination tasks, not simulation.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' with a V2 limits_scope label is not supported. The measure is a grouping/relevance proxy with unequal node budgets, not a share of single-job neurons. Neurons were described separately for positive and negative sign, which matches the essay's 'poles', but no per-pole interpretability share is reported. Appendix D also shows autointerp scores can be high while groups lack mechanistic content, a caution relevant to V6/V7-style debates, but it concerns transcoder supernodes, not neurons.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not audit Qwen3-32B or estimate the shares of poles with one job, two related jobs, or no understood job.

Only Gemma-2-2B is studied; the paper does not test dense and mixture-of-experts models across scales up to trillions of parameters. Its grouped-feature fraction is not the same measure as the claimed job-count shares.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example or recursive-generalization account is tested.
The study does not test the claimed architectural, regularization, or tool causes, nor the InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
The study does not establish that neuron attribution graphs explain behavior without a replacement model and reconstruction error.
It does not test whether neuron explanations based on activating examples predict firing on unseen text.
It does not score individual neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of raw MLP neurons assigned to supernodes by the automated annotation pipeline.
rows.measure: Fraction grouped into supernodes; pooled across graphs
rows.note: Table reports mean counts per graph of 32.1 grouped, 116.0 ungrouped, and 148.1 total MLP neurons. The grouped fraction is an annotation-pipeline outcome, not a direct estimate of the claim's one-job/two-job/unknown shares. Authors say this result suggests many MLP neurons do not have a clean concept.
rows.check: Supernode-grouping fraction (21.6%) reflects prompt relevance and pipeline grouping rules, not single-job interpretability of neurons. Node budgets differ (150 MLP vs ~44.6 transcoder), and the 150 was chosen to match grouped counts. The baseline is the transcoder rate, so the 'partial' state against V2's ~90% share is not meaningful.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of transcoder features assigned to supernodes by the same annotation pipeline.
rows.measure: Fraction grouped into supernodes; pooled across graphs
rows.note: Table reports mean counts per graph of 26.8 grouped, 17.8 ungrouped, and 44.6 total transcoder features. This is a comparison basis, not a direct measure of neuron job counts.
rows.check: Transcoder-feature grouping rate is a comparator for a different basis; it does not measure neurons.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-2-2B raw MLP neurons on the 100 Capitals graphs
reader_labels.reason: The pipeline groups 21.6% of raw MLP neurons, versus 60.2% of transcoder features, and the authors say this suggests many MLP neurons lack a clean concept; R1 and R2. These grouping rates are not directly comparable to the claimed job-count shares.
